https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: A Senate inquiry into the Albanese government’s gambling laws has heard allegations that betting companies and casinos are providing big spending punters with drugs, free accommodation and escorts. Anti-gambling campaigner Tim Costello told Monday’s hearing he was preparing to give a character reference to a man being detained in Sydney’s Silverwater prison, who was allegedly targeted by promoters. The man is preparing to plead guilty to charges over theft of more than $12m, Costello said. Costello alleged to the hearing that gambling companies including TAB and Sportsbet offered the man drugs, escorts, and free accommodation. He was given free accommodation at Star Casino. He had to leave each week so they could technically say he wasn’t living there and come back the next morning. He was the TAB’s biggest customer in that time. They were giving him $50,000 bonus bets. He was also Sportsbet’s biggest customer. They were flying him to grand finals. They were offering him escorts, drugs

Norfolk Police was called to South Beach Parade shortly after 00:30 BST on 16 May. Dawid Wlach, 35, of Dover Court in Caister-on-Sea, has been charged with one count of rape, one count of oral rape, one count of assault by penetration and one count of sexual assault. Wlach, who police said was a Polish national, has been conditionally bailed by police and is due at Norwich Magistrates' Court on Tuesday, 28 July. Another man appeared before magistrates in June and he is due at Norwich Crown Court, also on 28 July. Madalin Ilinca, 34, of Suffolk Place in Great Yarmouth, is charged with one count of rape, one count of sexual assault and one count of sexual assault by penetration. Ilinca, who police said was a Romanian national, has been remanded in custody ahead of a plea and trial preparation hearing at the crown court. Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/se.text: Loznitsa’s new documentary Imperium uses archival footage from the early 1970s filmed in the former Soviet Union. Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMOD View image in fullscreen Loznitsa’s new documentary Imperium uses archival footage from the early 1970s filmed in the former Soviet Union. Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMOD Venice film festival Ukrainian film-maker criticises EU after it cuts Venice Biennale funding over Russia controversy Sergei Loznitsa likens removal of €2m grant to ‘a punishment in kindergarten’ on eve of Venice film festival Philip Oltermann European culture editor Wed 2 Sep 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 04.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google One of Ukraine’s most acclaimed film-makers has criticised the European Commission’s decision to cut off funds to the Venice Biennale over the opening of Russia’s pavilion, likening it to “a punishment in kindergarten”. The Biennale drew heavy criticism this spring when it allowed Russia to use its pavilion for the first time since 2022, despite the ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Speaking on the eve of the Biennale’s cinematic branch, the Venice film festival , the director Sergei Loznitsa said that while he would “never ever” personally visit the Russian pavilion, the row was a distraction from the EU’s own failure to enforce more effective economic sanctions against Moscow. “The question I ask myself is this: can the existence of this Russian pavilion stop this war or not?” said Loznitsa, who won wide acclaim for his 2014 documentary Maidan and last year’s Soviet-set drama Two Prosecutors, and is showing his new film Imperium out of competition on the Lido this year. He added: “What I do know is that in the second quarter of this year, European companies imported gas from Russia at unprecedented levels, and all that money goes straight into bombs that fall on Ukraine .” View image in fullscreen Sergei Loznitsa at the Cannes film festival in May last year. Photograph: Kristy Sparow/Getty Images According to the EU’s Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators, European imports of Russian liquified fossil gas increased by 17% compared with the same period in 2025, before a full EU-wide ban on Russian gas from 2027. Loznitsa said: “This is a much more serious issue than whether there is a Russian pavilion in Venice or not. Cutting off funding to the Biennale is like a punishment in kindergarten.” While the Russian pavilion’s exhibition The Tree is Rooted in the Sky was only accessible during the pre-opening vernissage dates and has been closed to the public since 9 May, the European Commission confirmed last month that it was terminating its €2m (£1.7m) multiyear grant to the Biennale Foundation. The row is now also threatening to engulf the Venice film festival, which has a degree of institutional independence from the Biennale but will be directly affected by the funding cut. The Biennale’s management said the terminated grant used to co-finance the activities of the cinema department relating to Biennale College and the Venice Production Bridge affects “activities and a department that have nothing to do with Russia’s participation in the Biennale Arte”. In a confrontational speech before the announcement of this year’s lineup, the Biennale’s president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, accused the commission of “abandoning our journey”. The Biennale, he said, was not engaged in politics but “international research in the field of arts”. View image in fullscreen The president of the Venice Biennale, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, has led the criticism of the commission’s decision. Photograph: Stefano Mazzola/Getty Images For a festival that has in the past often looked more focused on attracting celebrity glitz than its competitors in Cannes and Berlin, this year’s programme is noteworthy for its political flavour and thematic focus on Russia and the countries in its sphere of influence. As well as Loznitsa’s Imperium, there is the French director Alexandre Smia’s geopolitical “disaster movie” Jupiter, in which the Russian president has survived an assassination attempt for which he blames Ukraine and seeks retribution. Andrei Kutsila’s animated documentary Letters from the Silenced Country focuses on political repression in Belarus, while the Russian-born American film-maker Julia Loktev’s five-hour documentary My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile follows a group of Russian dissident journalists working for the independent television channel TV Rain after they are forced to flee their country in the wake of the full-scale invasion. View image in fullscreen My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile stars Ksenia Mironova, left, and Valeria Ratnikova. Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film Festival Loktev’s film circles around the question of where art and journalism stops and propaganda begins. In one scene, the journalists working for TV Rain find themselves chastised for continuing to speak of “our army” after they have registered the network in Latvia. “It’s a film about when your country does terrible things, how to take accountability,” said Loktev. “How do you speak as a citizen of your country about the awful actions and the crimes your country is committing?” The inclusion of another Russian-themed film project, Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s Dau, has brought criticism from Ukrainian authorities. The Ukrainian ministry of foreign affairs raised “profound concern” over Khrzhanovsky’s film, which tells the story of the Soviet physicist who reluctantly contributed to the creation of the first atomic bomb. “Russia has long used culture as an instrument of state policy and hybrid warfare,” the ministry said in a statement. “For the Kremlin, culture is a way to restore to sanctioned figures the respectability that politics has taken from them; to legitimise its presence where tanks cannot reach; and to appropriate the history of the very lands it seeks to erase.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every week Sign up to Film Weekly Take a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that matters after newsletter promotion The ministry said that the multi-film Dau project, once described as a “Stalinist Truman Show”, has received funding from the Russian businessman Sergey Adonyev, who has been sanctioned by the US and Ukraine, and that its Greek-born protagonist Teodor Currentzis accepted Russian citizenship granted by Putin. View image in fullscreen A still from Imperium. Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMOD But in a social media post, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, Alberto Barbera, rejected the description of Dau, which was principally shot from 2008 to 2011, as a “Kremlin-financed project”: “[It] is not a Russian film; it is not pro-Putin propaganda,” he said. “It is a film that denounces totalitarian regimes and their intrusion into citizens’ lives to restrict their freedom.” Unlike at the Venice art biennial, directors showing their work at the film festival do not represent a country. Dau was funded by Germany, France and Sweden, while My Undesirable Friends was made in the US and Loznitsa’s Imperium has received financial support from Germany, Italy, France and Lithuania. The comments on the festival row by the Belarus-born, Ukraine-raised and now Germany-based Loznitsa are striking, not least because his own submission to the festival applies a strongly critical lens to the internal contradictions of Russian imperialism, the role of cultural propaganda and blindspots in how the Soviet Union used to be seen from the west – specifically from Italy. The three-hour film is solely based on archival footage shot by a group of Italian film-makers who, thanks to the blessing of the Italian Communist party, were allowed to make three filming expeditions to the Soviet Union between 1970 and 1973. View image in fullscreen The footage used to make Imperium was shot by Italian film-makers on an officially sanctioned visit. Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMOD With filming strictly supervised by KGB handlers, the footage they amassed was meant to project the unity of the Soviet empire, showing a sea of red flags on Moscow streets as the patriotic anthem Wide is My Motherland blares from speakers. Yet the further the crew travels into the outer reaches of the Soviet Union, the more the ambiguous the images become. Local customs, from throat singing to reindeer racing to village wrestling competitions, emphasise the disparity rather than the unity of Soviet culture. In the Yakut Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, local people watch on with visible scepticism as a group of urban young Russians parade through the streets with guitars and fiddles. “I wanted to show that the Soviet Union collapsed not just for economic reasons, but also because it was impossible to keep so many different cultures under one roof,” said Loznitsa. Moscow’s much-mythologised propaganda arm – still detected by many behind the cultural policies of the Russian state today – appears largely ineffective in Loznitsa’s film. In one scene, the camera hovers over a small tractor parading portraits of members of the politburo through a muddy and forlorn landscape in Dagestan. “It’s a bit like the Russian pavilion in Venice now,” the film-maker said. “As propaganda, it’s just so ridiculous.” Explore more on these topics Venice film festival Festivals Ukraine Europe Russia Venice Biennale news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://24.hu/belfold/2026/11/09/a-karpa.text: Kulcsár Krisztián beszámolt arról, hogy az ukrán parlament október 12-én elfogadta a nemzeti kisebbségek anyanyelvű oktatását megerősítő törvénymódosítást, amely a Tisza képviselője szerint fontos garanciát jelent a kárpátaljai magyar közösség számára. Elmondta, a jogszabály-módosítás időkorlát nélkül biztosítja a magyar nyelvű érettségi lehetőségét, és önálló jogállást ad a nemzeti kisebbségi oktatási intézményeknek. Kiemelte, hogy a Tisza-kormány tárgyalásos megközelítése hónapok alatt meghozta a várt áttörést. Velkey György külügyi államtitkár válaszában beszámolt a kárpátaljai oktatási megállapodás részleteiről, amelyek szerint a jogszabály révén bevezetik az ukrán jogrendbe a nemzetiségi kisebbségi intézményi státuszt. Ez még az egyosztályos iskolákban is lehetővé teszi a magyar anyanyelv használatát, a nemzeti történelem oktatását, valamint az identitás megőrzését. Az államtitkár kijelentette, hogy a kormány a konfrontáció helyett a megoldásorientált, párbeszédre épülő külpolitikában hisz. Hangsúlyozta egyúttal, hogy a határon túli magyarok jogainak biztosításáért a jövőben is következetesen kiállnak mind az anyaországban, mind azon kívül.
